Params: The database's faint blue light pulsed in silence, a ceaseless rhythm like the tireless beating of a mechanical heart.
She drew a slow breath. The reading had shifted by twenty percent since the day before. For an ordinary human, that would be well within normal fluctuation.
But her heart was mechanical, built to never tire, designed to beat with unwavering precision and hold its numbers perfectly steady.
Her body was a prosthetic built from the most advanced materials, the kind that required meticulous upkeep from a top-tier laboratory.
That it had endured this long at the bottom of the ocean was already a miracle.
But the physical world followed its own cold rules. The body was breaking down.
Manann drew out the syllables, stretching them long.
And that "annoying" sound coaxed a smile from Cordelia even as the dull pain gnawed at her body.
Cordelia, I opened a lot of basement bottles today.
It's a marine construction tradition. Schools send drift bottles with well-wishes inside, and they're released into the sea when the project is finished.
Every engineering robot carries a big batch when they set out. Mine was stored in the basement under the lighthouse.
But they haven't drifted yet. They've been in the basement this whole time.
The mechanical crab's logic was impeccable.
Stored in the basement, so they're basement bottles. And if you accidentally break one, I suppose it becomes a shatter bottle?
Mm... Before I came here, I did have a shatter bottle.
Correction. I possessed a shatter bottle.
There was a drawing inside, sent by a child named... Nanami. But a shatter bottle can't keep out seawater. By the time I saw the drawing, half of it was already ruined.
It was a damaged scribble, half-eaten by the sea.
Well, that's your fault for breaking the bottle.
Though the comms channel fell into silence, Cordelia could picture it clearly in her mind: a tiny, indignant face, cheeks puffed up with frustration.
(She's learned to throw a tantrum now...)
She was growing more and more like a human child.
No response? Then... should I rename you Manann Who Doesn't Speak?
The little crab's voice "darted" off the comms channel in a flash.
Now she's in her rebellious phase, huh...

Cordelia leaned back in her chair at the control console, a faint smile lingering on her lips. She reached for the coffee cup on the desk, and the sluggishness of her own motion drew another quiet sigh.
The malfunctions in her prosthetic body were growing more frequent. The nerve response in her left hand had degraded so badly that even gripping a cup took two or three attempts.
The daylight simulation lamp on the console had been dead for a long time now, much like the failing body she inhabited.
Cordelia, why aren't you talking to me?
Manann's voice piped up through the comms channel again.
I wasn't fighting with you. You were mad all by yourself.
Then I'll make up with you. By myself.
I took a painting out of one of the basement bottles.
There's an old human man in a little wooden boat. A huge fish is jumping out of the water next to him.
The fish is really big. But it doesn't look like the whale you talked about.
Cordelia found the matching picture in her memory at once.
That's not a whale. That's a marlin.
The story is called "The Old Man and the Sea."
A marlin? I wanted a whale story...
The sharp crack of breaking glass rang through the comms, one after another. Cordelia's brow furrowed.
Looking for a whale story. I'm going to find one in the shatter bottles.
On the distant surface of the sea, Mirage Island lurched into a brutal, shaking spasm.
I hate this. I don't feel good, Cordelia.
A strange, piercing screech tore through the comms channel.
A cold weight settled in Cordelia's chest.
She had noticed it some time ago. The Lighthouse was deteriorating, or more precisely, the makeshift filtration unit was failing.
Had the rising concentration of the virus already begun to affect Manann?
Activate every sensor you can access and send me your latest system logs.
A sad little face appeared on the screen from Manann.
Cordelia scrolled through each log, her finger finally stopping in the middle of the display. She did not lift it away.
That was all the answer Cordelia needed. She understood exactly what was unfolding before her and what those logs truly meant.
The Lighthouse's filtration was weakening. As the virus concentration crept steadily higher, the Punishing Virus's corruption edged closer to Manann's processing core.
The script of fate was turning to its last page.
Manann, how much longer can the Lighthouse's filtration hold?
This is not a game. I need you to answer me seriously.
From that moment on, time had an ending.
Cordelia, don't be scared. Even if I turn into a monster, I will never hurt you.
Of course you won't hurt me. I know it.
What do you want to hear today, Manann?
She held a decision deep inside, one she could not yet share with Cordelia, and it had stirred in her a rare and genuine curiosity.
I want to learn more about names.
You said my name... comes from mythology.
What is mythology? Is it your history? Your past?
No. Mythology isn't history. And it isn't the past.
It's not a record of what happened in history. It's the way humans once explained the world around them.
But even now, those stories still help a people understand their own lives and their own ways of thinking. In a way, they're still what holds us together.
Like the glory of Valhalla, the doomed fate of Ragnarok.
What am I like? In the mythology.
Well... a lot of the old stories have been worn down by time. Only pieces survive...
So it's lost? Hmph, that's boring.
A soft laugh escaped Cordelia before she could stop it.
Then... Gunnar and Larsen. Tell me their ancestors' stories... I like those two.
Their ancestors... that would be the age of the gods...
In the old tales, Odin received a prophecy of the world's end. Balder's death would plunge the world into an endless winter. After that, Ragnarok would begin.
In that story, fate was never a possibility. It was a single, irreversible road that allowed no turning aside. Even the gods, in all their greatness, could not slip free of its design.
But the gods are so powerful. Even they can't run away from fate?
She tilted her head back and gazed up toward the ocean's surface, as distant and unreachable as the heavens above. Her body was failing, drawing closer with each passing hour to the embrace of death.
After she was gone, only this clumsy machine would remain in these waters. A Manann who had awakened to consciousness and feeling, who had come to understand the true weight of loneliness.
She would have to face this vast ocean alone, until the Punishing Virus consumed her completely and transformed her into a complete monster.
Odin died in the jaws of Fenrir, the giant wolf. Balder's death was the ending fate had written from the very beginning...

Two years ago, when the Punishing Virus swept across the globe, Mannan should have already become a monster. Cordelia herself should have died in that apocalyptic storm and been laid to rest in the deep.
They had refused to surrender to fate's design without a struggle, and all the time they had clung to since then felt, in the end, like nothing more than borrowed days spent holding on to each other.
But fate's script now turned to the page that should have been read two years ago. The written ending no one could escape.
A human who stood at death's threshold, and a machine whose corruption was inevitable.
When I first walked into that port, I told that child the ocean isn't blue because the sky gives it its color. It's blue because the sea "ate" the red.
Her red hair kept its vivid color, even here at the bottom of the sea.
Fate... you hold a grudge, don't you?
Cordelia gazed at her own long red hair. She did not go on with the story of Ragnarok. A long, deep silence settled over her instead.
If you don't like this story, we can switch to another one...
Do you want news from Atlantis? I found some encrypted work logs in Jormungandr's files. They were never sent because the connection was cut off.
The fragments are hard to decrypt. I'm not finished yet...
It was... supposed to be your birthday gift, but I could give it to you early. You want to take a look?
In the current state of communications, both sending and receiving faced enormous obstacles. Any useful data she could find was extremely limited. Cordelia held out little hope.
This data packet is... supply logs... pretty boring.
This one... casualty list. This one's not good.
A sharp pulse jumped at Cordelia's temple.
Even with her stiff, mechanical way of thinking, Manann sensed the complexity of this moment.
The naive little mechanism did as the human asked.
The first thing she caught was Lybia's name.
Instinctively, she thought of the mechanical potted plant still sitting in the lighthouse on the Mirage Island, the cornflowers it had been growing meant for Lybia.
The file stated the cause of death plainly: a laboratory accident. The note was brief, the kind of lines found in any standard work report.
I remember her. You said she was a friend...
So... you already said goodbye to me. And I didn't even know.
The grief barely had a moment to take hold before a torrent of names struck her, one after another.
Row upon row of administrative staff.
And somewhere after a long, blurring litany, the logistics employees began to appear among the dead.
...Manann. Can you raise the temperature in the database a little?
A chill settled into her bones.
The list of fallen logistics personnel was not a long one.
And then the medical personnel's names began, one after the next.
Heavy as stones, they fell from her throat into the deep, invisible dark below.
Cordelia stopped the belated memorial before it could go any further.
That was enough for her to piece together what happened there.
<size=40>To share their human blood. To have once walked with giants.</size>
<size=40>This was the absolute compassion born from absolute reason.</size>
<size=40>And at this moment, such dazzling human brilliance, both tender and cruel, shone upon her in the lightless depths where no sunlight could ever reach.</size>
Cordelia slumped back into her chair and gazed up at the dome of the undersea database. The weight of the ocean pressed down upon her, immense and unrelenting.
(Even gods, for all their power, cannot escape their fate.)
Still decrypting the data packets, Manann searched desperately for something, anything, that might lift the young woman's spirits. And finally—
Cordelia... is this good news? Lybia... it seems she left a child behind.
I found a birth record in the appendix. It was a girl.
Her thoughts scattered, and her words lost all their order. She could no longer find any that could capture what she felt in that moment.
(Humans are so small... and still they throw themselves into the current.)
Even if nothing could be changed. Even if there was no way out.
Her voice broke just a little.
You asked me... why the gods, with all their power, can't run away from fate.
...Manann, when humans talk about fate, we don't really talk about escaping it. What we think about... is how to carry it.
We don't only make heroes of the ones who win. The ones who walk forward knowing exactly how the story ends... their souls shake us too.
I... don't want to talk about those...
Cordelia lowered her head, and her red hair fell forward to veil her face and the quiver of her lips.
I won't tell you stories that are scattered and worn, buried under the dust of time... I won't talk about the cycle of fate, or forces too vast to resist.
Manann, the age of the gods is long past.
She thought of the painting in the drift bottle, where the old man remained alone on his tiny wooden boat with nothing to show for his long journey.
I want to tell you about an old man who hasn't caught a fish in eighty-four days.
I want to tell you about how he sailed alone across the vast sea, waiting for the one great fish fate had reserved for him.
About his failures, stacked one upon another. About his face, weathered raw by the sea wind, and his hands, torn open by the fishing line.
About his body, pursued by age, and his soul, well acquainted with misfortune.
Manann, this is a story that belonged to humanity alone.
A human story of being beaten, broken... but not defeated.
A human story? What does that mean...?
(I know destruction is coming. And I... choose to stand against it anyway.)
I choose to rage against it.
I choose to rage against it.
Everything I sacrifice for it will decide who I am.
(Everything I leave behind will define who I am.)
In the days that followed, Cordelia rarely appeared on the comms channel.
Talking with Cordelia had become as constant a rhythm in her world as the daily tides.
When that voice suddenly vanished, Manann could no longer understand how time was passing.
She simply zoned out, waiting for the voice to return on the other end.
Manann's consciousness flickered to life in an instant.
Where did you go, Cordelia? I was so worried about you.
I thought you wouldn't show up today... It's the big day.
Cordelia hesitated for a moment, and then a faint, bitter smile crossed her lips.
I'd forgotten. That's perfect, then... I have good news, and a birthday is the right day to share it.
I fixed the deep dive pod.
That means you can leave! You can finally escape from the ocean! Right?!
Cordelia, you're going to be free!!!
Her voice came out thick, heavy with unshed tears.
Manann's mechanical mind could not yet grasp the weight behind those words. Her voice skipped across the comms channel, bright and happy.
Manann, will you come with me?
Of course you can! That's what I've been working on these days.
Your body is already corrupted. The overwrite program won't hold the virus back forever. One day, you'll turn into a monster completely.
So don't stay in that body any longer. I'm taking you out, Manann.
Out of the body the virus has claimed.
The Punishing Virus won't control your mind. You won't turn into a monster. You'll have a new body. You'll get to see the world outside.
A new world. The world... I lived in.
Manann's pitch lifted higher, a sure and simple sign of her happiness.
But... how do I do it?
In the tower on the island... I left a mechanical potted plant there.
It was made by my teacher, Dr. Kalon, just like you. When we used it to modify the lighthouse, the technology we used was part of the Mannan M-1A AI simulation system.
For now. I think we can use it as your new body.
My new body? It's so small, and... not very human.
She couldn't bring herself to finish.
I need to implant a separation program into your body. Then... you'll have to transfer yourself into the mechanical potted plant. Think you can manage that?
I can do it. I'm not scared. Pain doesn't scare me.
Cordelia, I want to go with you.
Then this is the best birthday ever! We have to celebrate it right!
Nearly all the instant food stored in the base had reached its expiration date.
The only thing left edible was tough, flavorless compressed biscuits, and eating one meant swallowing an entire bottle of water just to force it down.
Cordelia arranged the remaining compressed biscuits in a circle and lit the candles.
Its flame was small and unsteady, trembling in the dark.
She hummed softly to herself, the data streaming before her flickering in and out, her substitute for candlelight.
A birthday is a milestone given meaning, the day the world welcomed you into it. And what "Happy birthday" really means is... your existence matters to me.
I'm still alive. I still exist.
The button to shut down the database sat right there within her reach. One press, and the entire transoceanic cable network would go dark.
Her fingertips brushed over the cold button, as light as a touch upon the last bloom of a spring night before it withered.
Happy birthday. Thank you for having me... my homeland, my world.
Cordelia blinked, slowly drew her hand back, and offered a gentle smile.
What's the world outside like, Cordelia?
The polar snow lay thick and soft like a white blanket, and rising with the curl of chimney smoke was the warmth of a mother's simmering fish soup.
Tropical forests were an endless sea of green, and the air smelled like fruit ripening on the branch.
The sand burned hot under the sun, with golden dunes rolling endlessly away. When the wind stirred, it brushed past like silk whispering against the ears.
The water was as blue as the petals of the loveliest cornflower, a deeper, richer blue than even the sky above.
The world outside is vast and beautiful, Manann... You should go see it for yourself.
We... we'll see it together! I've watched many ads. There are so many places I want to go.
I want to go to the Copperfield Aquarium. I wonder if a mechanical crab like me would actually get caught if I showed up there...
Or we could go to the Venus Splash Park... but I think the rides are only built for human bodies.
Oh, wait. By then, I'll be a potted plant. The only question is whether I can get in without buying a ticket.
Since it's the last birthday, we have to make wishes properly.
Can I make lots and lots of wishes?
And Karenina, my big sister. I want to go to the park and the aquarium with her.
Mm... Manann, remember to find Karenina. Remember to find Kalon.
When you meet them... when you meet a stranger, smile first.
I'm sure they'll give you a pretty new body. And remember... be a good girl.
I want you to give me a new body, Cordelia.
I only want the body you give me, Cordelia. I want to be your child.
When we get to the new world, can I finally call you Mom? You never let me say it... That makes me not happy.
Then I'm making my real wish now.
Manann's words danced through the comms, bright with simple, childlike joy.
I want to be with Mom forever, not even a second apart.
The day they had marked arrived. It was the day when the Lighthouse's filtration would cease to function.
Outside, the weather was perfect and calm, the ocean a sheet of light beneath a cloudless sky.
Manann brimmed with excitement, the way a child looked forward to a long-awaited field trip.
Memory data extraction: 50%. Prepare to replace the upload vessel.
The little potted plant had been carefully placed onto the launch platform by a mechanical arm.
Cordelia—Mom! I'm going now. Don't take too long, okay?
This was likely the last time she would ever speak to Manann.
Cordelia? Mom... why do you sound like that?
The clumsy crab was slow to understand, but a faint unease had begun to stir inside her.
One last time, she hummed the lullaby.
Under its gentle, rocking rhythm, Manann's anxiety eased into quiet.
The ejection mechanism triggered. The deep dive pod shot up from the undersea base's secondary exit and climbed desperately toward the light above.
Manann's data core left the giant crab's body and transferred into the mechanical potted plant, launching toward the sea in tandem.
At the same moment, the deep dive pod's hull began to crack under the immense pressure of the deep.
The transmission cut out, and the humming fell silent.
Warning: Unauthorized deep dive pod activation. Damage rate: 87%. Destination adjusted: Machine landfill.
The deep dive pod had never been repaired.
The deep dive pod had never been repaired.
Understanding crashed over the clumsy crab all at once.
But on the other end of the line, the young woman would never answer her again.
I would have stayed with you at the bottom of the sea forever! I would never have left!
Please! Don't send me away, Cordelia!!!
The consciousness extraction program ran its course without mercy. Its mechanical logic was absolute: once initiated, it would not stop until a command ordered it to.
Cordelia's recorded voice came through as soft and gentle as it had always been.
Manann, I'm so happy that you won't become a monster.

It's just... I won't be there to walk the days ahead with you. You still have a long life to live. Now, you have all the freedom in the world to go wherever you want. The world is vast... but it's also small.
So vast you'd spend a lifetime and still be amazed by it. So small that... when you try to run from pain, there's nowhere to hide.
That's something you'll have to learn for yourself, Manann.
I lied to you, I know. But... your happiness matters more to me.
After you leave, your crab body... I don't know what it will become.
So I left instructions in the deep dive pod. A way to start the self-destruct sequence. If it ever loses control, that will be the last gentle thing we can do for this ocean.
Go and live a life that is completely, entirely your own.
And if one day you feel lonely, I know you'll still remember Kalon and Karenina.
I believe... you will find each other again.
In the midst of that unbearable pain, Cordelia had left her one last gentle comfort. It was so tender, so heavy with guilt and sorrow, that it only tore her "heart" into more pieces.
Cordelia... please, Mom... Mom! I don't want to leave you!
I don't care if I turn into a monster! If staying with you means becoming one, I don't care! I would've stayed, Mom!
She wailed like something damned, but all she had left was a thin, hollow voice that could change nothing.
<size=40>If only she had hands that could hold her mother and never let go.</size>
<size=40>If only she had eyes like a human's, eyes that could shed tears, that could show her mother all the dread, sorrow, and despair inside her.</size>
She must have looked monstrous, even terrifying. That was surely why Cordelia could not see how frightened and broken she was right now.
Mom... you don't like me anymore...?

Manann had never felt anything with such terrible clarity before. Everything she had ever known was tearing apart, shattering, grinding to dust, forcing a beast's anguished howl up from the deepest part of her mind.
Perhaps only humans could feel their own suffering so sharply, could name it so precisely.
And so, she felt a new world taking shape around her.
As she lost her ignorance, her fearlessness, her unawareness, a human "heart" began to grow inside her consciousness.
But in the very first second of its birth, that "heart" was met with annihilating pain. Every inch of it was already riddled with wounds.
Cordelia, what is the most important thing a human has to learn?
In that moment, Manann learned the final lesson of being human: the agony of powerlessness.
Gain and loss. Life and death. All the things humans could not control and could never change.
That strange, heart-rending pain would tear beastly howls from a human throat, and it would also stir human emotion in cold machinery.
How to live alongside such pain became the only question she had to face, now that she stood closer to being "human" than ever before.
Don't go somewhere I can never find you...

On that day, Cordelia asked what name she wanted. Formless logic was given shape, becoming reality, and a world came into being. From that moment on, every warmth life could offer and every sorrow it could inflict became hers to feel.
At the very beginning of the story, Mother brought the world to "me" from the void, and an ordinary machine was given a name to be called.
Now the mechanical potted plant's tiny metal claws gripped its base tight, and the island she had once carried on her back slowly receded into the distance.
The giant white tower dwindled against the sky.
The extraction procedure neared its end. The memories, the pain, all of it was fading away.
At the end of the story, Mother took my name away and told me that every living thing must learn to accept death.
At the end of the story, Mother took my name away and told me that every living thing must learn to accept death.
Merciful mother, all memory had left her.
Merciful mother, all memory had left her.

As the deep dive pod rose from the abyssal depths to the shallows, the pressure differential alone was enough to kill a healthy adult, let alone someone like Cordelia, whose ruined body had been propped up by prosthetics for so long.
From the very moment she had made her decision, Cordelia knew that the only thing returning to the island inside that broken pod would be her own corpse.
And yet... I feel happy. Because my story will end on the way home.
The pod climbed toward the surface. It had never been built for a return trip.
It had taken Cordelia when she ran from death's jaws.
It had taken Cordelia when she ran from death's jaws.
And now it carried her home to sunlight and soil, to the starting point of life itself.
And now it carried her home to sunlight and soil, to the starting point of life itself.
Will she... be a good girl?
In that final moment, before death's blade came down, the panic seized her at last, inevitable and all-consuming.
In that final moment, before death's blade came down, the panic seized her at last, inevitable and all-consuming.
What kind of person... will she become?
Death's veil had already swept across her face, cloaking the face that would soon rest in unending peace.
Death's veil had already swept across her face, cloaking the face that would soon rest in unending peace.
Did Mom feel the same when she left me? So worried and unwilling to go?
If fate had taken the form of a god,\nthen perhaps it was fate that had orchestrated everything, leading her to the very same ending her mother had met.
If fate had taken the form of a god, then perhaps it was fate that had orchestrated everything, leading her to the very same ending her mother had met.
Mom... I'm so close to you now, again.
I tried. I really did. But... living is not the best choice for me right now.
...Mom, I finally understand how you felt...
O Fate, Odin once received your prophecy of twilight. The gray raven once brought wisdom to endure the doom.
She murmured Larsen's poem under her breath, though it could scarcely be called poetry at all.
Are you real? You have to be real... Only if you're real can you hear me...
The deep dive pod broke the surface and slid along the rails toward the landfill. Five brief minutes in the open air, the last sunlight it would ever know.

Cordelia lay still inside that dark, lightless metal coffin. The pressure shift had been more than her fragile prosthetic body could withstand. It had destroyed this precious bloom raised in a greenhouse, though she had fought like a weed to survive.
Her final words still lingered in the close, silent air.
Odin once received your prophecy of twilight. The gray raven once brought wisdom to endure the doom.
Please hear me. Please grant my wish.
Let them become the most beautiful thing they can possibly be.
They said hearing was the last sense to leave when a person departed the world. Perhaps that was why, at the very end, she caught the bright, clear song of a bird.
A single tear slipped from the corner of her eye.
<size=40>Cordelia wanted to become a long road bathed in moonlight.</size>
<size=40>Moonlight, the color of pearls, of tears, of sorrow itself.</size>
<size=50>Cordelia, fate looked your way at last.</size>
<size=50>I hear you. I grant your wish.</size>
I hear you. I grant your wish.
Sunlight from thirty years away finally finds the still-wet tears of the one coming home.
Thirty years have passed. Mannan's body remains beneath the island, its base protocols still running, still executing commands written long ago, commands that will never receive a response.
It keeps its eyes open in the dark, feeling the currents shift, catching the distant cry of whales.
It has been waiting, without knowing for whom, without knowing for how long. But it will never stop waiting.
Once, a scientist bound for the moon came to it.
And once, a "god" came, one who granted its wish to become a "monster."
The little deep dive pod remains buried deep within its belly, because—
I want to be with Mom forever, not even a second apart.
<size=45>And at last, her soul finds its way back to her.</size>
<size=45>Merciful mother, all memory has returned to her.</size>
